title: A Feb-29 birthday plus 365 days is Feb 28 of the next year, not another Feb 29
assumption: Adding 365 days to a date gives you 'the same date, one year later'.

input.description: A 'renews annually' or '1 year from now' feature implemented as 'add 365 days' instead of 'add 1 to the year field'.

what_goes_wrong: A subscription or anniversary calculated as 'start date + timedelta(days=365)' for someone whose start date is February 29 lands on February 28 the following year, one day short of their actual next anniversary (which, in a non-leap year, does not exist on the calendar at all).
why: `timedelta(days=365)` counts elapsed days; it has no concept of 'the same date next year'. The 365 days after 2000-02-29 run from March 2000 through February 2001, a stretch with no leap day in it, so they end on 2001-02-28; 2001-03-01 is 366 days away. The same drift hits any date in a leap year that falls before Feb 29: 2024-01-15 + 365 days is 2025-01-14, not 2025-01-15.

repros.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

start = date(2000, 2, 29)
plus_365 = start + timedelta(days=365)
print("start:", start, "| +365 days:", plus_365)

fix: Decide explicitly whether 'in N years' means 'add N to the year field, clamping Feb 29 to Feb 28 (or rolling to Mar 1) if needed' or 'add exactly N*365.25 days'; use a calendar-aware date library's year-addition function (e.g. `dateutil.relativedelta`) rather than `timedelta(days=365)` for anything billed as 'annual'.
